title: American acts in postwar London and rationing
summary: She worked the London Casino with American acts and recalls ration packages and a feast with a friend.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: The Berry Brothers, the Nicholas Brothers, the Merrimacs -- all the American acts were living in this flat down there. This was when we were still doing the theater.
I opened at the London Casino, then we played the provinces and all around. And it was sort of rough there.
The Berry Brothers, they had been there, I guess a weeks before I got there. We all lived in the same flat.

And they had a party every night. Then one of the Berry Brothers went down to the delicatessen, whatever they call it, and got a chicken and put it on a table. But the chicken was only to be looked at. We couldn't eat it. (Laughs)

Oh boy oh boy! But see, Maurice Rocco, when he left here, it was all in the newspapers about all these trunks of food that he was taking with him. Steaks and all that. And I think that when the news got over there and he was in town, he had a following that you wouldn't believe.
But by the time I got there, it was all

gone! So I had some -- I guess you call them like CARE "care packages" sent to me. Your friends could send you food, you know.
And I remember my last day there, I had saved up my ration stamps and had a young girl working for me named Priscilla. A Scots girl, because she was showing me around --
I said, "Look, we're going to take our stamps. We're going to really have a feast. We're going to make a beef stew, get some beef and get some tomatoes"-- whatever goes in it.
And when she came back, I said, "Oh, if we just had some rice." She said, "Well my mother gets a barrel of rice once a year from China."
She called her mother up who lives outside of London, and her mother put a half of pound of rice on the train and sent it down to us.
So we cooked our -- we got a handful of shillings to put in the meter. We turned the heaters in the cooking stove, and we locked the door.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
knocking, the phone started ringing. I said, "Don't answer the phone and don't open the door!" That was my last meal in Scotland in '48.
But we had a feast. I had told Priscilla to get some corn on the cob. Corn on the cob is something that you don't --

But she came back with something that looked like a corn on the -- one ear. I said, "What is this, Priscilla?" She says, "That's the corn on the cob." I said, "How come you only got one?" She didn't even know how to order. I said, "Well I'll tell you what you do. You eat this ear of corn because I'm going back where I can get all the corn." Oh boy!
